claim: Mammalian body temperature fluctuates by about one degree over a span of 24 hr, a phenomenon called body temperature rhythm (BTR).
source: In humans, the phenomenon by which body temperature fluctuates by about one degree over a span of 24 hr is called body temperature rhythm (BTR).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about human physiology and is supported by citations.

claim: Body temperature rhythm is related to sleep from a physiological perspective.
source: From a physiological perspective, this body temperature rhythm is related to sleep.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations in the following sentence.

claim: When body temperature decreases at the transition from day to night, sleep latency increases.
source: For example, when body temperature decreases at the transition from day to night, sleep latency increases (Refinetti and Menaker, 1992; Aschoff, 1983; Kräuchi, 2002; Weinert, 2010; Gerhart-Hines et al., 2013; Kräuchi, 2007a, 2007b; Gilbert et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Little is known about the underlying relationships between sleep and body temperature in terms of neural regulation.
source: Little is known, however, about the underlying relationships between sleep and body temperature in terms of neural regulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Drosophila exhibit a daily temperature preference rhythm (TPR) in which their preferred temperatures increase during the daytime and then decrease at the transition from day to night.
source: We have previously shown that Drosophila exhibit a daily temperature preference rhythm (TPR), in which their preferred temperatures increase during the daytime and then decrease at the transition from day to night (night-onset) (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Drosophila achieve a body temperature rhythm (BTR) through their choice of environmental temperature because they are small ectotherms.
source: Because Drosophila are small ectotherms, they achieve a BTR through their choice of environmental temperature (Stevenson, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and draws on knowledge about ectotherms.

claim: The concept of BTR is not restricted to mammals and is likely evolutionarily conserved in mammals and Drosophila.
source: Therefore, the concept of BTR is not restricted to mammals, and it is likely that BTR is evolutionarily conserved in mammals and Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of BTR mechanisms between mammals and Drosophila.

claim: TPR is regulated independently from locomotor activity rhythms in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, our data suggest that TPR is regulated independently from locomotor activity rhythms because, while the dorsal neurons 2 (DN2s) function as a main clock to set the rhythmicity of TPR, PDF expressing lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) are not required for TPR during the daytime (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a previous study cited.

claim: DN2s function as a main clock to set the rhythmicity of TPR.
source: Interestingly, our data suggest that TPR is regulated independently from locomotor activity rhythms because, while the dorsal neurons 2 (DN2s) function as a main clock to set the rhythmicity of TPR, PDF expressing lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) are not required for TPR during the daytime (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PDF expressing lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) are not required for TPR during the daytime.
source: Interestingly, our data suggest that TPR is regulated independently from locomotor activity rhythms because, while the dorsal neurons 2 (DN2s) function as a main clock to set the rhythmicity of TPR, PDF expressing lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) are not required for TPR during the daytime (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: LNvs are important for locomotor activity, but DN2s are not.
source: On the other hand, LNvs are important for locomotor activity, but DN2s are not.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these neurons.

claim: In mammals, BTR and locomotor activity rhythms are regulated by different subsets of subparaventricular zone (SPZ) neurons.
source: Similarly, in mammals, BTR and locomotor activity rhythms are regulated by different subsets of subparaventricular zone (SPZ) neurons, suggesting that these rhythms are controlled independently as well (Saper et al., 2005a, 2005b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanisms of TPR appear to be distinct from locomotor activity mechanisms and resemble mammalian BTR.
source: Therefore, the mechanisms of TPR appear to be distinct from locomotor activity mechanisms and resemble mammalian BTR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mechanisms in Drosophila and mammals.

claim: Sleep and BTR have a close temporal relationship in mammals.
source: Sleep and BTR have a close temporal relationship in mammals and the mechanisms controlling sleep in flies are analogous to those in mammals (Crocker and Sehgal, 2010; Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The mechanisms controlling sleep in flies are analogous to those in mammals.
source: Sleep and BTR have a close temporal relationship in mammals and the mechanisms controlling sleep in flies are analogous to those in mammals (Crocker and Sehgal, 2010; Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: PDF-expressing small and large lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) play an important role in modulating sleep and arousal in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, pigment dispersing factor (PDF)-expressing small and large lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) play an important role in modulating sleep and arousal (Sheeba et al., 2008; Parisky et al., 2008) and morning anticipation in circadian locomotor activity rhythms (Allada and Chung, 2010; Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004; Yao and Shafer, 2014; Stoleru et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: PDF-expressing LNvs play an important role in morning anticipation in circadian locomotor activity rhythms.
source: In Drosophila, pigment dispersing factor (PDF)-expressing small and large lateral ventral neurons (LNvs) play an important role in modulating sleep and arousal (Sheeba et al., 2008; Parisky et al., 2008) and morning anticipation in circadian locomotor activity rhythms (Allada and Chung, 2010; Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004; Yao and Shafer, 2014; Stoleru et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Period mutants (per01) exhibit abnormal TPR during the daytime.
source: We previously showed that period mutants (per01) exhibit abnormal TPR during the daytime and that PERIOD expression in the PDF neurons did not restore normal TPR (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PERIOD expression in the PDF neurons did not restore normal TPR in period mutants.
source: We previously showed that period mutants (per01) exhibit abnormal TPR during the daytime and that PERIOD expression in the PDF neurons did not restore normal TPR (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pdf 01 mutants exhibit normal preferred temperature during the daytime.
source: Also, we recently showed that Pdf 01 mutants exhibit normal preferred temperature during the daytime (Goda et al., 2016), suggesting that neither PDF nor PDF neurons are required for regulating the rhythmicity of TPR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Neither PDF nor PDF neurons are required for regulating the rhythmicity of TPR.
source: Also, we recently showed that Pdf 01 mutants exhibit normal preferred temperature during the daytime (Goda et al., 2016), suggesting that neither PDF nor PDF neurons are required for regulating the rhythmicity of TPR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Pdf 01 mutants exhibit normal preferred temperature during the daytime.

claim: Pdf 01 mutants prefer a much lower temperature late at night before dawn (ZT16-24).
source: However, unexpectedly, we observed that Pdf 01 mutants prefer a much lower temperature late at night before dawn (ZT16-24) (Goda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: PDF neurons may be involved in regulating preferred temperature before dawn.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that PDF neurons may be involved in regulating preferred temperature before dawn.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Pdf 01 mutants prefer a much lower temperature before dawn.

claim: sLNvs, a subset of PDF neurons, are important for pre-dawn temperature preference at ZT22-24.
source: We reveal here that sLNvs, a subset of PDF neurons, are important for pre-dawn temperature preference at ZT22-24.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The morphology of sLNvs' projections varies across the day.
source: It has been shown that the morphology of sLNvs' projections varies across the day (Fernández et al., 2008; Sivachenko et al., 2013; Petsakou et al., 2015), leading to a temporal change in synaptic contacts with other neurons, which is controlled by the circadian clock (Gorostiza et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The morphology of sLNvs' projections leads to a temporal change in synaptic contacts with other neurons, which is controlled by the circadian clock.
source: It has been shown that the morphology of sLNvs' projections varies across the day (Fernández et al., 2008; Sivachenko et al., 2013; Petsakou et al., 2015), leading to a temporal change in synaptic contacts with other neurons, which is controlled by the circadian clock (Gorostiza et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: sLNvs contact and activate DN2s.
source: Our data suggest that sLNvs contact and activate DN2s, the main clock cells for TPR (Kaneko et al., 2012), and that these sLNvs-DN2s contacts dramatically fluctuate during the day and peak before dawn (ZT22-24).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: sLNvs-DN2s contacts dramatically fluctuate during the day and peak before dawn (ZT22-24).
source: Our data suggest that sLNvs contact and activate DN2s, the main clock cells for TPR (Kaneko et al., 2012), and that these sLNvs-DN2s contacts dramatically fluctuate during the day and peak before dawn (ZT22-24).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of temporal contacts between sLNvs and DN2s peak before dawn.
source: The number of temporal contacts between sLNvs and DN2s peak before dawn.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Thermosensory anterior cells (ACs) likely contact sLNvs via serotonin signaling.
source: Our data suggest that the thermosensory anterior cells (ACs) likely contact sLNvs via serotonin signaling.
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The ACs-sLNs-DN2s neural circuit regulates the proper setting of temperature preference before dawn.
source: Together, the ACs-sLNs-DN2s neural circuit regulates the proper setting of temperature preference before dawn.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: sLNvs are important for sleep.
source: Given that sLNvs are important for sleep and that BTR and sleep have a close temporal relationship, our data highlight a possible neuronal interaction between body temperature and sleep regulation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: BTR and sleep have a close temporal relationship.
source: Given that sLNvs are important for sleep and that BTR and sleep have a close temporal relationship, our data highlight a possible neuronal interaction between body temperature and sleep regulation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: There is a possible neuronal interaction between body temperature and sleep regulation.
source: Given that sLNvs are important for sleep and that BTR and sleep have a close temporal relationship, our data highlight a possible neuronal interaction between body temperature and sleep regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Inactivated PDF neurons caused a lower temperature preference than both Gal4/+ and UAS/+ controls at ZT19-21 and ZT22-24.
source: In these cells, we found that inactivated PDF neurons caused a lower temperature preference than both Gal4/+ and UAS/+ controls at ZT19-21 and ZT22-24 (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: UAS-Kir2.1/+ control flies preferred a lower temperature compared to Pdf-Gal4/+ controls.
source: Although UAS-Kir2.1/+ control flies preferred a lower temperature compared to Pdf-Gal4/+ controls (Supplementary files 1 and 2), the inactivation of PDF neurons caused a further significant decrease of the preferred temperature at ZT19-24 (Figure 1A green and blue stars, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: The inactivation of PDF neurons caused a further significant decrease of the preferred temperature at ZT19-24 compared to controls.
source: Although UAS-Kir2.1/+ control flies preferred a lower temperature compared to Pdf-Gal4/+ controls (Supplementary files 1 and 2), the inactivation of PDF neurons caused a further significant decrease of the preferred temperature at ZT19-24 (Figure 1A green and blue stars, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: An impaired endogenous clock in PDF neurons caused lower temperature preferences at ZT19-24.
source: An impaired endogenous clock in PDF neurons caused lower temperature preferences at ZT19-24 but similar temperature preferences to controls most other times of the day (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The circadian clock in PDF neurons is involved in regulating temperature preference before dawn.
source: Since these pre-dawn data are consistent with the phenotype of inactivation of PDF neurons (Figure 1B), we conclude that the circadian clock in PDF neurons is involved in regulating temperature preference before dawn.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Neither inhibition of PDF neurons, nor impairment of clock function in these cells disrupts temperature preference during the daytime.
source: Importantly, neither inhibition of PDF neurons, nor impairment of clock function in these cells disrupts temperature preference during the daytime (Supplementary file 3), which is consistent with previous findings that PDF neurons (LNvs) are not required for TPR during the daytime (Kaneko et al., 2012; Goda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 3 and citations to previous work.

claim: sLNvs and DN2s contact each other in the larval brain.
source: It has been shown that sLNvs and DN2s contact each other in the larval brain (Picot et al., 2009) and that sLNvs project near DN2s in the adult brain (Helfrich-Förster, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: sLNvs project near DN2s in the adult brain.
source: It has been shown that sLNvs and DN2s contact each other in the larval brain (Picot et al., 2009) and that sLNvs project near DN2s in the adult brain (Helfrich-Förster, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: sLNvs and DN2s are directly connected in the adult brain.
source: This raises the possibility that sLNvs and DN2s are directly connected in the adult as well.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that sLNvs and DN2s contact each other in the larval brain and that sLNvs project near DN2s in the adult brain.

claim: Reconstituted GFP fluorescence signals were observed only in the dorsal lateral area of the brain when flies had both split-GFP fragments expressed in DN2s and LNvs.
source: When flies had both split-GFP fragments (Clk9M-Gal4::UAS-CD4:spGFP1-10; Pdf-Gal80 / Pdf-LexA::LexAop-CD4:spGFP11), we observed scattered green fluorescence signals only in the dorsal lateral area of the brain (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), but not in the sLNvs somas nor the other regions of their projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no reconstituted GFP fluorescence signals in the control lines.
source: On the other hand, there were no reconstituted GFP fluorescence signals in the control lines (no green signal in Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: sLNv and DN2 projections physically contact.
source: These data suggest that sLNv and DN2 projections physically contact.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRASP experiment data.

claim: The number of sLNvs-DN2s contacts decreased during the daytime (ZT1-12).
source: Strikingly, while the number of sLNvs-DN2s contacts decreased during the daytime (ZT1-12), they dramatically increased during the night (ZT13-24) and peaked at ZT22-24 (Figure 2D, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, E and F.

claim: The number of sLNvs-DN2s contacts dramatically increased during the night (ZT13-24) and peaked at ZT22-24.
source: Strikingly, while the number of sLNvs-DN2s contacts decreased during the daytime (ZT1-12), they dramatically increased during the night (ZT13-24) and peaked at ZT22-24 (Figure 2D, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, E and F.

claim: Maximal axonal volume and spread of sLNvs projection are observed at ZT24.
source: These data are consistent with the recent finding that maximal axonal volume and spread of sLNvs projection are observed at ZT24 (Petsakou et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: GCaMP fluorescence in both sLNvs and DN2s increased upon the bath application of 3 mM ATP.
source: GCaMP fluorescence in both sLNvs and DN2s increased upon the bath application of 3 mM ATP (upper line, Figure 3A1 and B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A1 and B1.

claim: The fluorescence in sLNvs and DN2s did not change in response to vehicle controls.
source: In the negative controls, the fluorescence in sLNvs and DN2s did not change in response to vehicle (bottom line, Figure 3A1 and B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A1 and B1.

claim: The average increase over the baseline (∆F/F) in both sLNvs and DN2s in response to ATP was significant compared to the vehicle controls.
source: The average increase over the baseline (∆F/F) in both sLNvs and DN2s in response to ATP was significant compared to the vehicle controls (Figure 3A2 and B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A2 and B2.

claim: The excitation of sLNvs via P2X2 and the subsequent depolarization of sLNvs leads to a cytoplasmic calcium increase in DN2s.
source: The data suggest that the excitation of sLNvs via P2X2 and the subsequent depolarization of sLNvs leads to a cytoplasmic calcium increase in DN2s.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the calcium imaging data.

claim: sLNvs can contact and activate DN2s in a time-dependent manner.
source: Given that the GRASP experiments showed dynamic contacts between sLNvs and DN2s (Figure 2A), the data suggest that sLNvs can contact and activate DN2s in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRASP and calcium imaging data.

claim: DN2 inhibition caused lower preferred temperatures than controls at all times of the day.
source: Interestingly, we found that DN2 inhibition caused lower preferred temperatures than controls (Clk9M-Gal4/+; Pdf-Gal80/+, Clk9M-Gal4/+ and UAS-Kir2.1/+) at all times of the day (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: sLNvs activate DN2s to obtain a proper pre-dawn temperature preference behavior.
source: Because DN2 inhibition does indeed strongly cause the flies to prefer a lower temperature than controls, the data suggest that sLNvs activate DN2s to obtain a proper pre-dawn temperature preference behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: Inhibition of DN2s only changed the set point of TPR and not the rhythmicity of TPR.
source: Although DN2s are the main clock cells for TPR (Kaneko et al., 2012), inhibition of DN2s only changed the set point of TPR and not the rhythmicity of TPR.
evidence: This is an observation based on the behavioral data.

claim: In more than 80% of the flies, Clk9M-Gal4: Pdf-Gal80 and Clk9M-Gal4 were expressed only in one of the two DN2s in each hemisphere.
source: We found that in more than 80% of the flies, Clk9M-Gal4: Pdf-Gal80 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B) and Clk9M-Gal4 (data not shown) were expressed only in one of the two DN2s in each hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Silencing could lower only one of the two DN2 neurons' activities, which was insufficient to eliminate a rhythmic TPR since the other DN2 neuron can still drive a rhythmic TPR.
source: Therefore, we concluded that silencing could lower only one of the two DN2 neurons' activities, which was insufficient to eliminate a rhythmic TPR since the other DN2 neuron can still drive a rhythmic TPR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Clk9M-Gal4 is expressed in only one of the two DN2s in most flies.

claim: AC neurons are warmth sensors which control temperature preference behavior.
source: AC neurons are warmth sensors which control temperature preference behavior (Hamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: AC neurons project to the dorsal protocerebrum.
source: Interestingly, AC neurons project to the dorsal protocerebrum (Hamada et al., 2008; Shih and Chiang, 2011) where nerve fibers of clock neurons are enriched (Helfrich-Förster, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Nerve fibers of clock neurons are enriched in the dorsal protocerebrum.
source: Interestingly, AC neurons project to the dorsal protocerebrum (Hamada et al., 2008; Shih and Chiang, 2011) where nerve fibers of clock neurons are enriched (Helfrich-Förster, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Terminal projections of ACs are overlapped with dorsal projection of sLNvs.
source: The recent paper showed that terminal projections of ACs are overlapped with dorsal projection of sLNvs (Das et al., 2016), suggesting that in addition to contacting the DN2, sLNv neurons may also contact AC neurons at their respective distal termini.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: sLNv neurons may also contact AC neurons at their respective distal termini.
source: The recent paper showed that terminal projections of ACs are overlapped with dorsal projection of sLNvs (Das et al., 2016), suggesting that in addition to contacting the DN2, sLNv neurons may also contact AC neurons at their respective distal termini.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that terminal projections of ACs are overlapped with dorsal projection of sLNvs.

claim: Scattered, green fluorescent signals were observed in the dorsal area of the brain when flies expressed both split-GFP fragments in TrpA1SH-Gal4+ neurons and Pdf-LexA+ neurons.
source: When flies expressed both split-GFP fragments (TrpA1SH-Gal4::UAS-CD4:spGFP1-10 / Pdf-LexA::LexAop-CD4:spGFP11), we observed scattered, green fluorescent signals in the dorsal area of the brain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the control lines, when only one of the split-GFP fragments was expressed, there was no reconstituted GFP fluorescence signal.
source: However, in the control lines, when only one of the split-GFP fragments was expressed, there was no reconstituted GFP fluorescence signal (no green signal in Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: TrpA1SH-Gal4+ and Pdf-LexA+ neurons project to the dorsal protocerebrum and form contacts with each other.
source: The data indicate that TrpA1SH-Gal4+ and Pdf-LexA+ neurons project to the dorsal protocerebrum and form contacts with each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRASP experiment data.

claim: Only the sLNvs project to the dorsal area where AC neurons project.
source: While Pdf-LexA is expressed in both sLNvs and lLNvs, only the sLNvs project to the dorsal area where AC neurons project (Hamada et al., 2008; Helfrich-Förster, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A potential synaptic connection is likely between sLNvs and ACs.
source: This suggests that a potential synaptic connection is likely between sLNvs and ACs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only sLNvs project to the dorsal area where AC neurons project.

claim: Both input and output synapses were detected in the fiber projection of sLNv neurons in the dorsal protocerebrum.
source: It is important to note that both input and output synapses were detected in the fiber projection of sLNv neurons in the dorsal protocerebrum (Yasuyama and Meinertzhagen, 2010; Collins et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Dendrites of ACs are not observed in the dorsal protocerebrum area of the brain.
source: However, dendrites of ACs are not observed in this area of the brain (Shih and Chiang, 2011), indicating that AC axons project to the dorsal protocerebrum.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: AC axons project to the dorsal protocerebrum.
source: However, dendrites of ACs are not observed in this area of the brain (Shih and Chiang, 2011), indicating that AC axons project to the dorsal protocerebrum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dendrites of ACs are not observed in the dorsal protocerebrum.

claim: NP0002-Gal4 is more selectively expressed in the AC neurons than TrpA1SH-Gal4.
source: Although NP0002-Gal4 expression is weaker than that of TrpA1SH-Gal4, we found that NP0002-Gal4 is more selectively expressed in the AC neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) than TrpA1SH-Gal4 and is only expressed in a few other cells in the Subesophageal Ganglion (SEG) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1A2.

claim: A GRASP signal was observed in the same brain region as TrpA1SH-Gal4 and Pdf-LexA GRASP signals in NP0002-Gal4 and Pdf-LexA flies.
source: In NP0002-Gal4 (independent ACs driver) and Pdf-LexA flies (LNv driver), we observed a GRASP signal in the same brain region as TrpA1SH-Gal4 and Pdf-LexA GRASP signals, although the signals were very weak due to the lower expression of NP0002-Gal4 (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the GRASP experiment.

claim: ACs and sLNvs may have synaptic connectivity.
source: Because NP0002-Gal4 is expressed more specifically in AC neurons than TrpA1SH-Gal4, these data further support that ACs and sLNvs may have synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRASP experiment data.

claim: The inactivation of TrpA1SH-Gal4+ neurons caused the flies to prefer significantly lower temperatures than controls at ZT19-21 and 22–24.
source: We observed that the inactivation of TrpA1SH-Gal4+ neurons caused the flies to prefer significantly lower temperatures than controls at ZT19-21 and 22–24 (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: TRPA1 knockdown in ACs caused a lower temperature preference than both Gal4 and UAS controls before dawn (ZT22-24).
source: We found that TRPA1 knockdown in ACs caused a lower temperature preference than both Gal4 and UAS controls before dawn (ZT22-24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: TRPA1 knockdown in ACs by NP0002-Gal4 caused a similar lower temperature preference phenotype to that of TRPA1 knockdown in ACs by TrpA1SH-Gal4.
source: Furthermore, TRPA1 knockdown in ACs by NP0002-Gal4 caused a similar lower temperature preference phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1) to that of TRPA1 knockdown in ACs by TrpA1SH-Gal4.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: ACs are involved in regulating temperature preference before dawn (ZT 22–24).
source: Therefore, these data further support the conclusion that ACs are involved in regulating temperature preference before dawn (ZT 22–24).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: The inactivation of TrpA1SH-Gal4 expressing neurons caused a higher temperature preference than controls at ZT1-3.
source: Additionally, we observed that the inactivation of TrpA1SH-Gal4 expressing (TrpA1SH-Gal4+) neurons caused a higher temperature preference than controls (TrpA1SH-Gal4/+ and UAS-Kir2.1/+) at ZT1-3 (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: ACs are serotonergic.
source: ACs are serotonergic (Shih and Chiang, 2011), and LNvs express one of the serotonin receptors, 5HT1B, that contributes to circadian photosensitivity (Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: LNvs express one of the serotonin receptors, 5HT1B, that contributes to circadian photosensitivity.
source: ACs are serotonergic (Shih and Chiang, 2011), and LNvs express one of the serotonin receptors, 5HT1B, that contributes to circadian photosensitivity (Yuan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: 5HT1B knockdown in PDF neurons caused lower temperature preferences than the controls at ZT16-18 and ZT22-24.
source: 5HT1B knockdown in PDF neurons caused lower temperature preferences than the controls at ZT16-18 and ZT22-24, but these flies preferred similar temperatures as controls during the rest of the day (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 5HT1B knockdown using R6-Gal4 caused lower temperature preferences before dawn at ZT19-21 and 22–24.
source: Consistent with the phenotype of the 5HT1B knockdown using Pdf-Gal4 (Figure 4E), 5HT1B knockdown using R6-Gal4 caused lower temperature preferences before dawn at ZT19-21 and 22–24, and similar temperature preferences as controls during the rest of the day (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 5HT1B expression in sLNvs is required for proper setting of temperature preference before dawn.
source: Therefore, our data indicate that 5HT1B expression in sLNvs is required for proper setting of temperature preference before dawn.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: The ACs-sLNvs neural circuits via serotonergic transmission likely contribute to temperature preference before dawn.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that the ACs-sLNvs neural circuits via serotonergic transmission likely contribute to temperature preference before dawn.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral and anatomical data.

claim: TrpA1SH-Gal4 > Kir2.1, TrpA1SH-Gal4 > TNT, TrpA1SH-Gal4 >TrpA1-RNAi, and control flies showed normal temperature entrainment to 20°C: 25°C temperature cycles.
source: The behavior of flies in which the AC neurons had been silenced (TrpA1SH-Gal4> Kir2.1, TrpA1SH-Gal4> TNT) or depleted of TRPA1 (TrpA1SH-Gal4>TrpA1-RNAi) seemed very similar to that of wild type and control flies, indicating that AC neurons are not required for temperature entrainment to 20°C: 25°C TC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AC neurons are not required for temperature entrainment to 20°C: 25°C temperature cycles.
